bibliography.abstract: ABSTRACT Urban parks play critical roles in balancing biodiversity conservation and public recreation, yet the multifunctional demands they face frequently create tensions between ecological objectives and recreational uses. In practice, prioritising one goal can constrain the other, and managers must mitigate the resulting disadvantages while conserving urban biodiversity. This study investigates the strategies that park managers use to manage biodiversity conservation–recreation trade-offs across five nature-oriented parks in Saitama Prefecture, Japan (Kamogawa Mizubenosato Park, Sayama Hill Flora & Fauna Interaction Centre, Saitama Green Forest Museum, Kitamoto Nature Observation Park, and Ageo Maruyama Park). These strategies are grouped into three analytically derived orientations: Environmental Focus, Balanced Focus, and User Focus. A mixed-methods approach integrating text mining, co-occurrence network analysis, and thematic content analysis of semi-structured interviews was employed. A novel 30-level Conservation and Utilisation Management Framework was developed that classifies management orientations, defined here as managers’ dominant strategic direction for handling conservation–recreation trade-offs. Orientations are associated with external environmental conditions (e.g., land-use context), internal site characteristics (e.g., scale and naturalness), and management perspectives (e.g., policy mandates and partnerships). Across all sites, user communication methods, including regulation, collaboration, and experiential programming—played a central role in reconciling conservation with recreational use. This analytical framework provides a practical and adaptable tool for diagnosing park governance orientations, guiding policy development, and integrating biodiversity conservation and recreational objectives in urban and peri-urban park management.
bibliography.title: Balancing biodiversity conservation and recreational use in nature-oriented parks in Saitama Prefecture, Japan

en.caveats: The framework and management orientations were developed using a small sample of five specific parks within a single Japanese prefecture, which may limit its immediate applicability to different national or institutional park systems.
en.what: This study analyzes how park managers navigate the trade-offs between ecological preservation and public recreation across five nature-oriented parks in Saitama Prefecture, Japan. Using text mining, co-occurrence network analysis, and thematic content analysis of semi-structured interviews, the researchers developed a 30-level Conservation and Utilisation Management Framework that categorizes park management into Environmental, Balanced, or User Focus orientations.
en.why: It provides a diagnostic tool that links a park's strategic management orientation to its external land-use context, internal naturalness, and policy mandates. This allows park administrators to systematically evaluate and adjust their governance strategies, particularly through targeted user communication and collaborative programming, to better reconcile ecological goals with public use.
